Findings.Title: First-ingress recovery still lacks a durable session identity before its write-ahead record
Findings.Defect: The first-ingress diagram writes the failsafe mint record before it assigns the previously absent mcpSessionId. It then records the new ID only in the enclosing single Update-TurnState change, whose durable replace occurs after OpenTurnUnderLock returns. This contradicts the guarantee that the write-ahead root envelope already contains the stable session ID and that a crash before the open is confirmed cannot change it.
Evidence: Update-TurnState applies the change, then writes/flushed-renames the file (538, 544-547). OpenTurnFromPromptHook explicitly makes the whole open one such change (1022, 1027, 1039-1042).

The current edge order is WA Write-ahead failsafe mint record -> FI no mcpSessionId recorded -> FIW Record a new mcpSessionId in this replace -> Invoke-SessionOpen (1056-1059). At WA a first-ingress host has no session ID to put in its required root envelope.

A kill after WA or after the server open/mint but before the outer replace leaves the recovery record without the promised durable binding, or leaves the host state without that ID. A later start can allocate a second session instead of replaying the original pair. Moving an in-memory assignment before the network call does not create a durable boundary.

StartHostSession itself is repaired: its standalone Update-TurnState completes before Invoke-SessionOpen (1391-1392). Final-refusal retention is also repaired (1047). The remaining defect is the first-ingress path, so AR1-F6 and its inherited R4-F8/R3-F6 chain are only partially resolved.
Findings.SpecificChange: Make the first-ingress session-ID allocation a durable, completed atomic state write before both the failsafe mint record and any open/mint call. Then write the full immutable recovery envelope and perform the open/mint. Reconcile the one-replace/lock wording and both diagrams with those explicit boundaries; add crash cases after ID persistence, after the write-ahead record, and after a lost open/mint reply that prove the same session/request binding is recovered.
Findings.Regression: AR1-F6 remains NOT RESOLVED; final-refusal retention and the standalone SessionStart path pass, but the first-ingress durability claim still does not.

Findings.Title: Missing GraphRAG documents can remain permanently unprojected after reconciliation
Findings.Defect: ReconcileProjectedDocuments returns a Projected row with a missing document to Pending but never clears GraphRagDocumentId or ProjectedContentSha256. ProjectOneResponse skips ingestion solely when the projected hash equals ContentSha256, independent of row state or document existence. The newly Pending row still has that matching hash and is skipped forever.
Evidence: The projection model keeps both the document ID and projected hash (2851). Reconciliation only says back to Pending (3690, 3740), while promising the next pass ingests it again.

Counterexample: a trusted response has Projected(D,H), document D disappears, and reconciliation sets State=Pending. The next pass selects the row (2852), reaches the hash-equality guard (3713), and exits Continue (3714), without calling IngestTextAsync. Subsequent reconciliation considers only Projected rows, so it does not repair this Pending row.

The live GraphRagService allocates a fresh document ID on ingest and lists/deletes documents separately (a8d3934b, GraphRagService.cs:343-379,411-448,488-492); no service operation implicitly clears the relational projection hash. The design trace is archived in 20261013T174659Z-architecture-counterexamples.json.
Findings.SpecificChange: Define the missing-document reset to clear the obsolete document ID and projected hash, or make the skip condition require a confirmed current Projected document. Apply the same invariant to every transition that can lose/remove a document, and add a two-pass case asserting a new document is actually ingested and the row becomes Projected after reconciliation.
Findings.Regression: The original AR1-F7 orphan cleanup obligation is now represented by the GraphRAG store and reconciled, but its new missing-document repair path introduces this regression.

Findings.Title: Supersede retries fail after the replacement changes status
Findings.Defect: Supersede promises that repeating the same replacement returns 200 unchanged, but both its activity and sequence validate the replacement current status before checking whether the original was already superseded by that replacement. A legitimate subsequent lifecycle change makes a previously applied request fail on retry.
Evidence: Counterexample: A is superseded by B, then B is superseded by C (or B is rejected). Retry the successful request A -> B. B is now Superseded/Rejected, so 3533 and 4557-4558 return 409 agent_context_supersede_invalid before reaching the already-by-this-replacement 200 branch at 3535/4561.

3515-3516 explicitly promise a repeat naming the same replacement returns 200 unchanged; the plan derives SupersedeRepeatSameReplacementReturns200Unchanged at 983. The current ordering cannot satisfy that promise for a valid chain.
Findings.SpecificChange: Inside the serialized/locked operation, recognize the already-applied original/replacement pair and return its stored unchanged result before mutable replacement eligibility checks. Apply those checks only to a new transition; retain whole-turn-key validation, rejection of another replacement, and cycle protection. Add retries after the replacement is subsequently superseded and rejected.
Findings.Regression: Holistic finding outside the original AR1-F3 whole-turn-key counterexample; that identity repair itself passes.

Findings.Title: The token budget does not account for rendered findings
Findings.Defect: The only token accounting is the per-item byte estimate and the sum/subtraction of item tokens. The canonical renderer additionally emits a line for every contradiction/blocker finding, but the architecture defines no token charge or reserve for those lines. Mandatory item tokens equal to the entire budget are explicitly accepted, so a package with such items plus a finding exceeds its stated bound under the same estimator.
Evidence: 2687 defines ceil(utf8ByteCount / BytesPerToken) per item; 2733 puts TokenCount on items. Findings are separate records with a summary up to 2048 characters (2770-2771), not counted items.

3078 emits finding lines after the items and says mandatory tokens equal to the budget build. FillBudgetWithCandidates tests/subtracts only the candidate tokens (3153, 3162-3163). No final rendered-size check is defined.

Even granting that each item estimate includes its header, four mandatory item segments totaling 1024 estimated tokens plus a 256-byte finding at BytesPerToken=4 yield at least 1088, while the current rule accepts the 1024-budget build. This is a design arithmetic trace, not an assertion about a tokenizer or future implementation.
Findings.SpecificChange: Define the estimator over all content the bounded package renders, including headers, separators, and finding lines. Reserve/count mandatory rendering overhead before the overflow decision and account for optional-item-induced findings during budget fill; preserve the explicit overflow and deterministic replay rules. Add exact-boundary cases with a contradiction and a blocker so the serialized/rendered package cannot exceed the configured estimate.
Findings.Regression: Holistic completeness defect affecting the attached plan bounded-package/explicit-overflow promise; it is not a demand to replace the accepted deterministic estimator with a model tokenizer.

Findings.Title: Post-commit response orchestration is repeated across units without its required shared component
Findings.Defect: The grade units, Reject, Supersede and EvaluateStaleness all receive the same post-commit algorithm: detect qualifying status transitions, select response/package dependents, check Mode, dispatch staleness before projection, and log/swallow dispatch failures. It is stated globally, but no section 3.5 component owns and encapsulates that algorithm, exposes its seam, or has its one test class. IDispatcher only dispatches the supplied request; it does not implement this selection, ordering, or failure policy. ResponseStatusTransition is explicitly inside the database transaction, so it cannot itself be this post-commit orchestration under the stated contract.
Evidence: 180 names five classes of caller and the complete shared dependent-selection/dispatch rule; 182 adds the shared projection scheduling/failure rule. 3045 repeats both as obligations of those units rather than a call to a named component.

Section 3.5.5 names ResponseStatusTransition, IResponseStalenessRule, ResponseIdList and RelationshipWriter, but none owns these post-commit steps. The ownership and seam lists at 5451 and 5456 likewise name only each command dispatch.

The operator rule at 22 and 141 requires logic shared by multiple units to be encapsulated as one section 3.5 component, not merely documented once. The new dependency propagation is functionally appropriate, but its implementation boundary is missing.
Findings.SpecificChange: Add one named post-commit response-effects component in section 3.5 with an owner, namespace/folder, input/output/error contract and one test class. It should own dependent selection, Mode checks, ordering, dispatch/failure handling and projection scheduling; each committing unit calls it once with the committed transition set. Keep the actual EvaluateStaleness and ProjectAgentResponses operations as their existing CQRS units.
Findings.Regression: The AR1-F2 dependency-status fix introduces additional shared orchestration without carrying it into the DRY component catalog; the original recursive staleness rule itself is repaired.
